en: And when prey appeared a bush-length away,
He sprang without swerving aside.
His tail was distinctive and his spirit fierce,
His frame colt-like and his back straight,
His straddling legs were like ravines,
And the white blaze upon his brow was like a tooth,
Like steel beaten by a smith.
His poll was like a ewer,
His triple-folded withers
Could bear a six-span cauldron
If the precious vessel were set upon it.
When fat, he was slender as a lance,
When leaping, nimble as a flea,
His calf was thick as a child’s waist,
And his stride was like the wind of the highlands.
A wild ass that swerved aside,
He could turn and trample as though devouring it.
No winged thing could flee and escape him,
And unless a dark calamity befell,
No enemy in battle could capture him.
Kulunsur, the thoroughbred steed,
Chewed barley when it was given,
A creature of splendid animal form,
Whose eyes shone like an argali’s.
He cracked wheat beneath his teeth;
Perfectly fashioned Kulunsur,
Whose eyes shone like a wild ram’s.
That day, precious lion Seytek
Took off his saddle and left him bare-backed.
With a great hobble fitted with golden handles,
He hobbled and tethered him,
Securing him with an extra tie.
He drew in the ill-fated steed’s flesh
By tying him down tightly.
His tether was golden at the hitching place,
Glittering and gleaming,
While in Akbermet’s palace
Seytek reveled in boundless delight.
For ten days Seytek did not stir,
The hapless, radiant hero,
But lay with the fairy maiden.
Your noble-born Bermet—
The purest wearer of a flowing gown,
Whose speech no words could equal,
Was herself the foremost among women.
Her brow was radiant and her words were gold,
Her tongue was sugar, the finest nightingale,
And when you looked upon her, she was the brilliant Morning Star.
Modest and fair-browed,
No mortal being could compare
With the unfortunate noble-born Bermet,
Created unlike all others.
As she lay sleeping that night,
She dreamed a wondrous dream,
And saw this magnificent portent.
She saw her dream clearly,
And beheld the full moon;
To her right she saw the sun,
And they were immersed in great delight.
Then, as her dream continued,
A fierce lion and panther
Came into Seytek’s possession.
They mauled whatever attacked,
And destroyed whatever they encountered;
No creature withstood their ferocity,
And the earth burned wherever they passed.
Seytek seized them by their collars,
While every living creature
Found no grave in which to hide,
And no earth into which to enter.
Scorched, the sand curled into drifts,
And wolves fled in panic, howling;
All creatures despaired of life.
A black eagle seized its prey,
And a collared sighthound followed the trail;
He built a fortress at Kakan
And slaughtered everything he unleashed them upon.
That eagle he had flown
Had eyes like opened pits,
And a beak like a steel auger;
Its beak gaped wide,
Its talons spread broad,
And blood flowed wherever it struck.
All the fanged beasts—
Lions and wolves that devoured—
Burned in helplessness
And fled into the gorges.
Through the four corners of the world
He made four complete circuits,
Hunting game with hawk and hound,
And reveled in this great delight.
Through the five quarters of Medina
He made five complete circuits,
And in every known place
He brought all things to completion.
“The warrior is Seytek,” they said,
And the whole wide world learned his name.
He challenged the panther
And grappled with the tiger.
Whatever he encountered he bent beneath him,
And that eagle carried it off.
Rejoicing in the deeds
And pleasures of his hunt,
He wearied his horse and surveyed the land,
Hooding and then flying his bird,
Yet never reached his intended destination.
Before this Seytek
No one remained who dared object.
Then, as she slept, she dreamed again:
The valiant panther Seytek
Found two blades of steel.
The sign of those blades was this:
When swung, they never recoiled from stone,
And from any place struck against an enemy
They never returned without shedding blood.
Their sheaths were beautifully fashioned;
Seeing how keen the steel was,
The great smith and forefather David
Looked upon it and praised it.
Roving on reconnaissance in high spirits,
He encountered a dragon
As huge as Mount Kap-Too.
The matched pair of keen swords
Could not prevail against the dragon,
And fire could not pierce its breath;
They fought but could not overcome it.
With a roar it swept from the east
And came to rest in the east.
Scorching the face of the earth,
That dragon charged.
Grappling with it, leopard Seytek
Vanished from this world.
Unable to overcome the fierce one,
Only a spoonful of blood remained,
Only a bruised scrap of flesh remained.
The sword shattered at the hilt,
The heart burst from its sheath,
The fiery heart was stirred,
The Ala-Too where the people dwelt
Was reduced to dust and turmoil.
The fire they kindled was extinguished,
The countless Kyrgyz, vast as a cliff,
The ravenous brute sucked them dry
And drove them all away.
It mauled whoever it encountered,
And devoured whoever crossed its path,
Leaving this land ownerless,
Leaving many women widowed,
While its hostile people settled there.
Plunged into calamitous misery,
The ancient nation was massacred;
Everything that so much as stirred
Was swallowed from the east.
The crops they had sown
Were reaped raw before they ripened.
Whoever dared resist
Was swallowed like tribute and sucked dry.
The sword broke in the middle,
And vanished from sight;
Of that ill-fated disaster,
No one knew where it had gone,
It plunged daylight into night,
And whoever dared resist
Was cast into a pit with no return.
The Kyrgyz of this Ala-Too
Were trapped in a precious net
From which no struggle could free them.
“What could this mean?”
So then that
Ill-fated Perizada,
A peerless mistress of wisdom,
Recounted her many-colored dream,
Telling all its wonders;
Lady Perizada’s
Clear account was thus.
Sobbing bitterly, she began to speak,
And spoke in anguish:
Some parts were blissful, others grievous,
One was hell and one was paradise;
She told the whole dream she had seen.
When he had heard this dream,
Valiant leopard Seytek
Rose and stirred from sleep,
Alarmed for his beloved people,
Wondering what would follow,
And saddled Kulansur.
“For one whose mount prances proudly,
May his road be fortunate when he rides;
If it rears and strains against the rein,
May it not chafe his hands.”
A finely knotted, perfect halter,
Fitted superbly just so,
A halter made exactly for Kulansur.
A leather saddlecloth and blue saddle blanket,
A white bearskin saddle pad,
A fitting pad for a hero’s mount,
Its pommel of pure gold,
Its rear entirely of silver,
Iron plates along both sides,
Crafted with consummate skill;
While his princely father still lived,
Bölökbay, master of the forge,
Had made it as a final bequest.
Can one who fears death ever prosper?
In this fleeting mortal world,
Can anyone possess an iron soul?
Thinking this, brave Seytek
Took the inherited white saddle, saying,
“Let the hero saddle up and ride;
If a mighty challenger comes,
If a foe comes who can uproot mountains,
Let him enter battle without retreating;
Let him drive out his enemy’s soul
And rout them all together;
May it never chafe his back,
Nor trouble the heart of its rider;
Though he journey for six months,
Though he ride the horse hard and long,
Though he travel day and night,
Let him not falter when battle begins;
This white saddle was specially made
So it would not press the horse’s flanks.
May those who come after Bölökbay
Know his meticulous skill;
When they remember him in desperate straits,
May they think of us.”
The White Saddle, fashioned with such care,
Was set upon Kulansur,
But the dear lion, proud as a cock,
The valiant hero, did not stir.
The lady took his hand and embraced him,
And softly spoke:
“What fate awaits him?”
He lay back without stirring,
Revealing himself a lion among lions;
The dark-blue warrior took no heed,
But rejoiced at the thought of death.
Akjoltoy, son of Kutubiy,
Whose valor equaled countless troops,
Whose figure led the vanguard,
Whose presence loomed in peril,
Whose path was blessed when he went ahead,
Who, when an implacable foe came
And threatened his entrusted life,
Alone was equal to countless troops,
Mounted a horse like Kulansur,
Put on his coat of tempered iron,
Prepared his arms and took his spear,
And girded on his naked sword.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
He took a spear without a tassel,
Turned its point and hastened
To brave Seytek’s palace,
To Perizada’s fortress;
Gray-maned Joltoy now arrived.
